objective: P1 mid-frequency engine Stage 0 (measurement, promotion-only): for the 53 fast signals already in the equity-book signal store, seven new daily fast signals and three fast composites, measure on U3000 by liquidity bucket the daily industry- and beta-neutral rank-IC decay (lags 1..22), persistence, half-life and net Sharpe versus trading speed at a close fill with cost model v1, and promote to the Stage 2 book-level test the objects whose recent-window implementable information is significant.

sources.core_claim: Guijarro-Ordonez, Pelger and Zanotti (Deep Learning Statistical Arbitrage, arXiv 2106.04028): on about 550 liquid US stocks, out of sample 2002-2016, the Sharpe ratio of the learned residual stat-arb policy has a half-life of about seven trading days over the holding period, is still above one at a 22-day holding period with a 1-day objective, and reaches about 1.5 when the multi-day holding period is optimized directly (Figure 12).
sources.project_applicability: Sets the trading-speed grid (kappa 1..0.05, full rebalance every 5 or 21 sessions) and the lag range 1..22 of the decay curve; Stage 1 of P1 replicates this model.
sources.reflection: Authors' backtest, ends 2016, 5 bp per transaction plus 1 bp short fee; learned signal, not the linear library signals measured here.

sources.core_claim: Da, Liu and Schaumburg (NY Fed Staff Report 513; Management Science 2014): the standard short-term reversal profit decomposes into across-industry momentum, within-industry expected-return variation, under-reaction to within-industry cash-flow news and a residual; only the residual is significant and positive, and a strategy built to capture it earns a risk-adjusted return three times the standard reversal over 1982-2009.
sources.project_applicability: Motivates IREV5 (within-industry reversal) and RREV5/RREV21 (risk-model residual reversal) next to raw REV5.
sources.reflection: Monthly reversal, 1982-2009, gross of costs; our test is daily on 2017-2026 U3000 with measured close costs.

sources.core_claim: Gervais, Kaniel and Mingelgrin (The High-Volume Return Premium, JF 2001): stocks with unusually high (low) trading volume over a day to a week tend to appreciate (depreciate) over the following month; the effect is stronger when the volume shock is not accompanied by an extreme return.
sources.project_applicability: Defines VSHK with a positive sign; our proxy is the 21-day over 63-day dollar-volume ratio (coarser than the paper's one-day to one-week shock).
sources.reflection: NYSE stocks 1963-1996, gross; our volume proxy is coarser than the paper's measure.

sources.core_claim: Garleanu and Pedersen (Dynamic Trading with Predictable Returns and Transaction Costs, JF 2013): with costly trading and signals of different decay speeds, the optimal portfolio trades partially toward an aim portfolio that weights slower-decaying predictors more.
sources.project_applicability: The speed grid uses the GP partial-trade form w_t = (1 - kappa) w_(t-1) + kappa w*_t; the decay curves give the alpha decay that GP needs for Stage 2.
sources.reflection: Our Stage 0 uses one kappa per signal, not the full GP aim portfolio across signals.

sources.core_claim: Novy-Marx and Velikov (A Taxonomy of Anomalies and Their Trading Costs, RFS 2016): for most anomalies a buy/hold spread is the most effective cost mitigation; for very high turnover strategies a combination of techniques does better.
sources.project_applicability: Stage 0 measures the partial-trade (kappa) family only; the buy/hold band is a Stage 2 construction variant, named here so it is not forgotten.

sources.core_claim: Lou, Polk and Skouras (A Tug of War: Overnight Versus Intraday Expected Returns, JFE 2019): momentum profits accrue overnight and partly reverse intraday, while other anomaly returns accrue intraday, so overnight and intraday components of past returns carry different information.
sources.project_applicability: Motivates ON5 and ID5 as separate inputs; the paper gives no clear sign for a 5-day component predicting total close-to-close returns, so their signs are fixed on the stress window before the recent window judges them.
sources.reflection: Monthly portfolios, 1993-2013; our components are 5-day means on 2017-2026.

sources.core_claim: Avellaneda and Lee (Statistical Arbitrage in the US Equities Market, Quantitative Finance 2010): residuals of stock returns on PCA or sector-ETF factors are traded as mean-reverting processes; after transaction costs PCA-based strategies have an average annual Sharpe ratio of 1.44 over 1997-2007 but only 0.9 over 2003-2007, and ETF-based strategies 1.1 with a similar degradation after 2002.
sources.project_applicability: RREV5/RREV21 use the project's risk-model residuals (industry + style factors) as the residual definition; the OU-threshold rule itself is a Stage 1 baseline, not measured here.
sources.reflection: 1997-2007; thresholds and costs differ from ours.

sources.core_claim: Attention Factors for statistical arbitrage (arXiv 2510.11616): with 5 bp per transaction, the parametric (OU-style) residual model falls to negative net Sharpe because of turnover, a simple PCA factor model reaches about 1.5 net, and the end-to-end model with costs in the objective reaches about 2.3 net (authors' backtest, 500 US stocks to 2021).
sources.project_applicability: Shallow single-signal or threshold rules fail on costs; Stage 0 therefore measures speed curves and composites, and P1 Stage 1 puts costs into the objective.
sources.reflection: Authors' own backtest ending 2021; flat 5 bp costs.

sources.core_claim: Frazzini, Israel and Moskowitz (Trading Costs of Asset Pricing Anomalies, NBER draft 2012, AQR live executions): size, value and momentum survive costs at fund sizes of tens of billions, while short-term reversal does not survive at sizes above about $9 billion in the US.
sources.project_applicability: Reversal is cost-constrained at institutional size but our book is small (E = $1M for impact), so the binding cost is the spread; Stage 0 uses the measured close half-spread by stock and year.
sources.reflection: Institutional execution 1998-2011; capacity, not small-account economics.

sources.core_claim: Project regimes study (2026-10-01): daily open-to-open, full daily rebalance, industry- and beta-neutral long-short returns of the fast library signals have recent-window gross Sharpe up to 2.64 (g191_gtja190; a101_alpha016 1.56) but annual turnover of about 70-260 times gross, so at a flat 8 bp per side most are deeply negative net (a101_alpha016 -4.15); m0_composite is 1.81 gross, 1.53 net.
sources.project_applicability: The fast library carries daily information that the monthly-horizon T-24 screen could not see; costs at full daily rebalance kill it, so Stage 0 measures decay and trading speed with measured close costs instead of re-testing single signals.
sources.reflection: Flat 8 bp, open execution, full rebalance, all U3000; diagnostic, not a selection input.

sources.core_claim: Blitz, Huij, Lansdorp and Verbeek (Short-term residual reversal, Journal of Financial Markets 16(3) 2013, 477-504; abstract from the Erasmus repository record): a reversal strategy on Fama-French residual returns avoids the dynamic factor exposures of conventional reversal and earns twice its risk-adjusted return; it is significant net of trading costs even for large caps after 1990.
sources.project_applicability: Second independent source for RREV5/RREV21; supports measuring residual reversal on the liquid L12 bucket with net costs.
sources.reflection: Abstract only (full text not opened: EFMA draft unreachable, SSRN not fetched); monthly horizon, sample ends about 2010.

sources.core_claim: Turnover-Adjusted Information Ratio (arXiv 2105.10306): extending the fundamental law with IC volatility and turnover cost, the turnover-adjusted IR is always below the cost-free IR, and managers can raise IR by limiting or optimizing turnover, against the naive implication of the fundamental law.
sources.project_applicability: Frames Stage 0's output: decay and persistence set turnover, so net Sharpe is read along the speed curve, not at full rebalance.
sources.reflection: Derivations and simulations; no market sample.
